sources.title: Immunometabolomics Applied to Physical Exercise: Accomplishments and New Directions for Health Improvement
sources.authors: Luciele Guerra Minuzzi; Alex Castro; Claudia Regina Cavaglieri; Ana Valéria Colnaghi Simionato
sources.population: Narrative coverage across health and disease; abstract highlights evidence from human trials, without fixed population eligibility or a single target cohort.
sources.design: Annual Review narrative review; no systematic review protocol or reproducible search method identified in the accessible article record.
sources.exercise_context: Exercise effects across time, tissue and modality, during and after exercise; acute and adaptation contexts are discussed broadly.
sources.biomarkers: Immunometabolic metabolites including succinate, itaconate, lactate, short-chain fatty acids and kynurenine; metabolomics and multi-omics methods. Traditional immune markers are not charted as a comprehensive panel.
sources.key_finding: Frames metabolites as links between energy metabolism and immune regulation and emphasizes time-, tissue- and modality-specific exercise responses.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No defined post-exercise infection incidence or URI endpoint is reported in the abstract/article scope inspected.
sources.validation: Discusses human-trial evidence and methodological advances; does not establish validated individual infection-risk prediction performance.
sources.limitations: Broad narrative treatment of immunometabolism rather than a map of post-exercise immune vulnerability; no systematic eligibility, marker-by-marker evidence chart, or infection outcome synthesis identified.
sources.evidence_anchor: Publisher abstract and publication information; PubMed publication type and identifiers.
sources.integrity_notes: The review is within the cutoff. PubMed labels it Review; publisher abstract explicitly calls it a narrative review. No obvious correction/retraction record surfaced in the targeted public-web check.

sources.title: Non-coding RNAs in exercise immunology: A systematic review
sources.authors: Mona Kotewitsch; Melina Heimer; Boris Schmitz; Frank C. Mooren
sources.population: Healthy human exercise-study populations with varied activity/training levels; not athlete-only. In-vitro validated target databases were additionally used to map immune targets, not as exercise intervention cohorts.
sources.design: PRISMA systematic review and qualitative synthesis; PROSPERO CRD42023408388; searches in PubMed, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus, with two complementary search strategies and reference checking.
sources.exercise_context: Acute and chronic/endurance and resistance exercise responses are separated; chronic evidence includes exercise programs and habitual training comparisons.
sources.biomarkers: miRNAs, lncRNAs and circRNAs, with immune target pathways; expression and assay platforms include sequencing, microarray and qPCR.
sources.key_finding: Synthesized 95 studies reporting 164 miRNAs; identified six studies on lncRNA/circRNA. Endurance miRNAs had consistency categories, but resistance evidence and functional interpretation remained limited.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No direct infection incidence or pathogen-confirmed infection endpoint synthesized; discusses immune pathways and function as biological relevance.
sources.validation: Classifies miRNA consistency as validated/plausible/suggestive based on repeated directional findings; this is not clinical biomarker validation or validated infection prediction.
sources.limitations: Omics/epigenetic layer only; no conventional marker panel, no infection outcome synthesis, and no full cross-scale open-window evidence map. Expression shifts do not by themselves establish changed immune function.
sources.evidence_anchor: PubMed abstract; full-text Methods (search and eligibility) and Results/flow diagram.
sources.integrity_notes: The issue date is May 2024 although electronic publication was November 2023. PROSPERO number is stated in the full text.

sources.title: Towards Precision Sports Nutrition for Endurance Athletes: A Scoping Review of Application of Omics and Wearables Technologies
sources.authors: Leon Bedrač; Leon Deutsch; Sanja Terzić; Matej Červek; Julij Šelb; Urška Ašič; Laure M. G. Verstraeten; Enej Kuščer; Filip Cvetko
sources.population: Endurance athletes; some CGM studies also include people with diabetes. Distance runners were the most represented group.
sources.design: PRISMA-ScR/PCC scoping review of original English-language research; PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation searching; 52 studies included; PEDro used for RCT quality assessment.
sources.exercise_context: Endurance sport, nutrition interventions, recovery and CGM; not structured as a post-exercise immune-window review and not a systematic acute-versus-training immune comparison.
sources.biomarkers: Metagenomics, nutrigenetics, metabolomics, multi-omics, proteomics, epigenomics, lipidomics and glucose wearables; plasma, stool and other matrices. Conventional immune-marker panels are not its organizing focus.
sources.key_finding: Maps 52 studies and makes clear that ‘scoping review + omics + precision/endurance athlete’ is already an established combination; many studies remain proof-of-concept with weak links to performance, recovery or long-term health.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No infection outcome was identified in the review text; outcomes were nutrition, performance, recovery and health parameters.
sources.validation: Assesses RCT quality using PEDro, but reports insufficient links between candidate biomarkers and meaningful outcomes; no immune-infection prediction validation.
sources.limitations: Nutrition-centered PCC and endurance athlete focus; it neither maps exercise immune status/function nor integrates sIgA, NK function, immune-cell kinetics, infection events and immune multi-omics.
sources.evidence_anchor: PubMed abstract; full-text Methods (search window, PCC and eligibility), Results and Discussion.
sources.integrity_notes: Confirmed as a peer-reviewed 2024 Nutrients scoping review, 16(22):3943, DOI 10.3390/nu16223943; it is not an exercise-immunity review.

sources.title: Impact of exercise on markers of B cell-related immunity: A systematic review
sources.authors: David Walzik; Sergen Belen; Karen Wilisch; Marie Kupjetz; Silvana Kirschke; Tobias Esser; Niklas Joisten; Alexander Schenk; Sebastian Proschinger; Philipp Zimmer
sources.population: Adults aged 18 or older, healthy participants and patients; multiple ages, health states and exercise backgrounds across included studies.
sources.design: PRISMA systematic review, PROSPERO CRD42021245527; MEDLINE, Web of Science and Embase searched 2023-03-08; controlled/non-randomized controlled and crossover trials; 67 studies (22 acute, 45 training).
sources.exercise_context: Acute endurance/resistance exercise and structured exercise training are analyzed separately.
sources.biomarkers: B-cell counts/proportions, plasma immunoglobulins, salivary/secretory IgA, salivary flow and secretion rate; no omics panel.
sources.key_finding: Acute studies often show within-session changes, but only a few differ from control. Training results are heterogeneous; some IgA outcomes rise while most remain unchanged versus controls.
sources.clinical_endpoint: Infection protection is discussed as a rationale, but direct infection incidence was not among the review's extracted outcomes and causality is explicitly uncertain.
sources.validation: Trial quality/reporting assessed with TESTEX; review concludes evidence confidence is limited and recommends functional B-cell outcomes and larger studies.
sources.limitations: Narrow B-cell/humoral marker scope; clinical infection outcomes and omics are not synthesized; review restricted to controlled/crossover designs and adults.
sources.evidence_anchor: PubMed abstract; full-text Methods (eligibility/search), Results and Discussion/Conclusion.
sources.integrity_notes: The issue publication date is May 2024 although the article appeared online in October 2023. Its stated PROSPERO registration was verified in the review text.

sources.title: The effects of acute and chronic exercise on immune markers of TH1/TH2 cells in older adults: a systematic review
sources.authors: Thiago Henrique Teodoro; Katerine Palharini Manfrin Costa; Jonato Prestes; et al.
sources.population: Older adults; diseased patients, animal studies and isolated-cell studies were excluded.
sources.design: PRISMA systematic review; PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, ScienceDirect and Scopus searched through March 2024; PROSPERO CRD42021244426; 14 studies, 525 participants.
sources.exercise_context: Three acute-exercise studies and eleven chronic/training studies; explicitly asks whether post-exercise immune alteration can characterize the ‘open window’.
sources.sampling_times: Acute IL-4, IL-6 and IL-10 measured immediately post-exercise and returned to baseline within 1 hour in the reported synthesis; chronic outcomes included after 24 weeks.
sources.biomarkers: Th1/Th2 cytokine and CD4/CD8 balance markers, including IL-4, IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α and CD4/CD8; no omics.
sources.key_finding: This is a direct framework-level neighbor that the prior collision report missed: it names the open-window question and synthesizes acute plus training markers, but only for older adults and one immune axis.
sources.clinical_endpoint: Infection susceptibility is background/rationale; actual infection incidence or pathogen-confirmed infection was not an included outcome.
sources.validation: ROB2 quality assessment; no biomarker diagnostic or infection-prediction validation.
sources.limitations: Older-adult subgroup only, restricted Th1/Th2 marker set, 14 small/heterogeneous studies, no traditional-plus-omics integration and no direct infection outcome.
sources.evidence_anchor: Full-text Abstract; Introduction (open-window rationale); Methods; Results 3.1 and Conclusion.
sources.integrity_notes: Directly refutes the prior report's categorical statement that no systematic review had applied an open-window framing. The review is narrow and does not duplicate the full proposed PCC. Registration identifier is stated in the paper.

sources.title: Rigorous methodological approaches to address knowledge gaps in exercise, nutrition, immunity, and infection risk research
sources.authors: Glen Davison; C. Chidley; A. W. Jones
sources.population: General population and athletes, including people exposed to exercise-related occupational stress; no fixed review inclusion population.
sources.design: Invited review/recommendations article; no systematic database search or evidence-map method identified in the article inspected.
sources.exercise_context: Exercise and nutrition research in acute and training/athlete contexts, viewed through URTI risk and study-design rigor.
sources.biomarkers: Critiques reliance on ex-vivo immune markers and recommends in-vivo integrated immune measures, pathogen screening and validated URTI logs; no multi-omics survey.
sources.key_finding: Argues biomarker changes can diverge from infection risk and recommends clinically relevant outcomes, in-vivo markers, larger samples and stringent controls.
sources.clinical_endpoint: URTI symptoms, pathogen-confirmed infection and viral load are recommended as primary/clinically relevant outcomes; the article is methodological guidance rather than an endpoint meta-analysis.
sources.validation: No new marker validation; offers research-design recommendations and explains limits of mechanistic ex-vivo endpoints.
sources.limitations: Not a systematic review or biomarker inventory; focuses heavily on nutrition-intervention research, but materially constrains claims that a marker change equals infection risk.
sources.evidence_anchor: Publisher Abstract, article type/date; full-text discussion of ex-vivo/in-vivo markers and URTI outcomes.
sources.integrity_notes: Publisher identifies this as an Open Access Invited Review, first published 2025-07-25. It is not a systematic review of candidate exercise biomarkers.

sources.title: Higher risk of upper respiratory tract infection post marathon running: when physical exercise becomes a threat to the immune system
sources.authors: Amanda Veiga Sardeli; Rafaela Bertini de Araujo; Jeffery A. Woods; Janet M. Lord; Mara Patrícia Traina Chacon-Mikahil
sources.population: Human marathon runners; within-person pre/post marathon comparisons of URTI symptoms.
sources.design: PICOS systematic review/meta-analysis; MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and EBSCOhost searched 2022-12-01; PROSPERO CRD42022380991; seven studies pooled.
sources.exercise_context: Single marathon event with symptom follow-up from one to four weeks; not multi-day training or biomarker sampling.
sources.sampling_times: URTI symptom follow-up 1–4 weeks; baseline and post-race follow-up durations were adjusted to align.
sources.biomarkers: No biomarkers synthesized; clinical symptom outcome only.
sources.key_finding: Meta-analysis estimated an 18% higher post-marathon URTI incidence (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.05–1.33), with moderate certainty and important limitations in measurement/confounding.
sources.clinical_endpoint: Self-reported URTI symptoms; no pathogen verification. Directly informs the infection-outcome layer but not biomarker prediction.
sources.validation: GRADE level reported as moderate; adjustment for unequal follow-up is a strength, but symptom subjectivity and time-varying confounding remain.
sources.limitations: Only marathon exposures and seven studies; does not measure immune markers, test marker-outcome links, or estimate post-exercise vulnerability in broader exercise settings.
sources.evidence_anchor: Journal abstract: methods, eligibility, synthesis, limitations and PROSPERO identifier.
sources.integrity_notes: Publisher page gives exact publication date and PROSPERO number. This is clinical infection evidence, not a biomarker review.

sources.title: The impact of exercise on inflammatory biomarkers: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
sources.authors: Wei Zhang; Minghui Du; Zhiyuan Zhang; Yixing Zhan; Longwei Chen; Jie Dong
sources.population: Broad health-status populations, including healthy adults, athletes/long-distance runners and multiple chronic disease groups; not athlete-only.
sources.design: Registered umbrella review CRD420251236842; PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and Cochrane searched through 2026-01; two reviewers; AMSTAR 2 and GRADE; 61 meta-analyses/318 exercise-biomarker-population associations.
sources.exercise_context: Mix of acute exercise and longer-term exercise interventions across included meta-analyses; explicitly cautions against interpreting chronic disease adaptations as acute responses in healthy people.
sources.biomarkers: Circulating inflammatory markers, especially CRP, IL-6, TNF-α and IL-10; no multi-omics or comprehensive immune-function panel.
sources.key_finding: Finds substantial population and design heterogeneity; evidence certainty is mostly low/very low, and acute physiological marker changes must be distinguished from chronic inflammation reduction.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No infection-incidence synthesis; focuses on inflammatory biomarker associations.
sources.validation: Assesses certainty of underlying meta-analyses using AMSTAR 2 and GRADE; no individual infection prediction validation.
sources.limitations: Umbrella-level biomarker evidence is broad, often chronic/disease-oriented and not post-exercise immune vulnerability; indirect comparisons and low certainty limit conclusions.
sources.evidence_anchor: PubMed abstract and Frontiers full text: Methods, Results, discussion of population heterogeneity and acute/chronic distinctions.
sources.integrity_notes: Publication date 2026-08-25 precedes cutoff. The stated PROSPERO identifier was verified in the full text.

sources.title: Circulating Myokine Responses to Acute Endurance Exercise and Their Role in Immunoregulation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Miriam Ringleb; Fabian Fabritius; Jakob Godde; Christian Puta; Wilhelm Bloch; Florian Javelle
sources.population: Healthy adults aged 18–50; illnesses, injuries and older adults excluded. Included participants were predominantly male (80%).
sources.design: PRISMA 2020, PROSPERO CRD42024535364; MEDLINE/PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and SPORTDiscus searched 2024-06-13; 167 studies in systematic review, 148 in meta-analyses, 3,622 participants across 294 interventions.
sources.exercise_context: Single acute endurance bout of at least 20 minutes; only immediate post-exercise sample within five minutes retained. Training interventions excluded except acute bouts embedded in a program.
sources.sampling_times: Same-day pre-exercise and immediate post-exercise within five minutes; later follow-up excluded.
sources.biomarkers: Serum/plasma IL-6, IL-10, IL-1ra, TNF-α, IL-15, IL-7, IL-8, TGF-β1 and fractalkine; conventional protein/cytokine markers, no omics platform.
sources.key_finding: Immediate acute endurance exercise increased six pooled myokines; response size varied by exercise dose, modality, age, sex, sample and training-related factors. Heterogeneity and risk of bias were substantial for some outcomes.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No infection incidence or pathogen-confirmed endpoint; acute biochemical changes were the outcome.
sources.validation: Dose/moderator analyses and GRADE evidence rating, not clinical predictive validation. Only a five-minute post-exercise window was analyzed.
sources.limitations: Immediate endpoint only, no recovery time course beyond five minutes, no chronic adaptation or infection-risk assessment, and underrepresentation of women.
sources.evidence_anchor: PubMed abstract; publisher/PMC Methods 2.1–2.2, Results 3.1–3.4 and Conclusion.
sources.integrity_notes: The article's DOI contains 2025, but PubMed/publisher issue and publication date are 2026-02; include as 2026 evidence. Registration CRD42024535364 is stated in the full text.

sources.title: Change in neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio after acute and chronic exercise: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Shokufe Khanzade; Sanam Mohammadzadeh; Farzad Fayedeh; Richard K. Shields
sources.population: Human participants of any age and health status; not limited to athletes or healthy adults.
sources.design: PICO systematic review/meta-analysis; PROSPERO CRD420251042422; PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane Library; 26 studies and 1,203 participants.
sources.exercise_context: Within-person NLR response to acute and chronic exercise; broad modalities and health states pooled.
sources.sampling_times: Immediately after and 1–3 hours after acute exercise; chronic training pre/post.
sources.key_finding: Pooled NLR did not change immediately after acute exercise, increased at 1–3 hours, and decreased after chronic exercise; heterogeneity was very high (I² approximately 94–98%).
sources.clinical_endpoint: No exercise-related infection follow-up; NLR's relevance to infection in other clinical contexts is not evidence of post-exercise infection prediction.
sources.validation: Sensitivity and publication-bias analyses reported; no individual-level model or infection-risk validation.
sources.limitations: Single simple marker, mixed healthy/patient populations and exercise contexts, very high heterogeneity, no omics or clinical exercise-related infection outcome.
sources.evidence_anchor: PubMed publication metadata and abstract; APS publisher full text/abstract, search and PICO methods.
sources.integrity_notes: Published 2026-08-01 despite a 2025 suffix in the DOI; within cutoff. PROSPERO CRD420251042422 is stated in the paper.

findings.claim: The prior collision report's categorical claim that no recent systematic review uses an open-window framing is not supportable: Teodoro et al. (2025) explicitly frames whether acute exercise causes an open-window period and systematically maps acute/chronic Th1/Th2 markers in older adults. It is a narrow neighbor, not a full-scope duplicate.
findings.protocol_implication: Replace ‘no review has addressed the open window’ with a qualified comparison: an older-adult Th1/Th2 systematic review directly discussed that framework, while the proposed review would map broader human exercise contexts, immune-marker classes and omics, and separately chart function, infection linkage and validation.

findings.claim: Recent reviews already cover both the ncRNA immune-omics layer (Kotewitsch 2024) and the scoping-review/precision/athlete/omics combination (Bedrač 2024). Novelty cannot rest on being first to map exercise immune ncRNAs, first to use a scoping review, or first to map omics in athletes.
findings.protocol_implication: Differentiate through cross-layer synthesis in the post-exercise immune-perturbation context, explicit infection outcomes, time-resolved sampling and an evidence ladder from concentration/expression through immune function to clinical association and validated prediction.

findings.claim: Marker change, immune function and infection incidence remain distinct endpoints. The B-cell review notes uncertain causal links; Davison et al. warns that ex-vivo marker shifts need not align with URTI risk; the marathon meta-analysis assesses symptoms without markers or pathogen confirmation.
findings.protocol_implication: Retain separate charting fields for biomarker concentration/expression, functional assay, self-reported illness, medically assessed illness and pathogen-confirmed infection. Do not infer infection risk from a changed biomarker alone.

findings.claim: Acute timing is a material scope decision: a 2026 systematic review restricts synthesis to samples within five minutes, while a 2026 NLR meta-analysis reports a different signal at 1–3 hours. A blanket exclusion of samples before 30 minutes would discard evidence needed to map immediate kinetics.
findings.protocol_implication: Remove the arbitrary under-30-minute exclusion or justify it against the research question. Chart exercise/≤5 min, 6–29 min, 30–60 min, 1–3 h, 3–24 h, >24 h and training-cycle periods separately; retain infection follow-up as a separate time scale.

findings.claim: The nearest recent literature is fragmented by scope: immunometabolomics narrative synthesis (Minuzzi 2026), ncRNA systematics, conventional B-cell/Th1-Th2 reviews, broad inflammatory-marker umbrellas, acute myokine synthesis, and a clinical marathon-URTI meta-analysis. No single verified record in this limited public-web scan integrated these layers and outcomes together.
findings.protocol_implication: Treat the remaining contribution as a provisional synthesis gap, not proof of a first-ever review. Recheck PROSPERO and databases with a librarian-built strategy immediately before protocol registration and again before manuscript submission.

findings.claim: The collision report contains material citation/type errors: its Hacker et al. 2023 item is an original study in BioMed Research International (49 participants, repeat acute endurance trials, biomarkers and 24-h recovery/performance prediction), not a Translational Sports Medicine narrative review. Its ‘Immunometabolism’ reference misattributes authors: the article is Nieman, Lila and Gillitt (2019), not Nieman and Wentz.
findings.protocol_implication: Correct the reference list and classify Hacker et al. as original research. Treat its individual recovery prediction as adjacent evidence only: it did not validate infection-risk prediction. Verify every cited reference against PubMed/publisher metadata before retaining the previous collision report's conclusions.

findings.claim: The prior collision report discloses ‘simulated databases’ rather than reproducible live database exports, and its 2026 re-assessment omits at least the 2025 Teodoro systematic review. Its ‘no collision/first review’ verdict therefore exceeds the evidence shown.
findings.protocol_implication: Do not reuse the previous novelty claim as established fact. Mark novelty as provisional pending the formally documented multi-database restart search.

gaps: No verified 2024–2026 source in this lane combines conventional immune indices and multi-omics candidates with human post-exercise time courses, immune-function assays, infection outcomes and individual predictive validation; the limited search cannot establish global absence.

Recent review evidence repeatedly separates immediate acute biomarker changes from chronic training adaptation, while the proposed protocol currently merges these unless charting strata are operationalized.

Clinical infection outcomes are measured in a narrow set of event-based studies and often rely on subjective symptom reporting; biomarker-to-infection associations and pathogen-confirmed prediction remain under-mapped.

Precision-biomarker claims need operational criteria: within-person repeatability, a defined target outcome, discrimination/calibration, external validation, and evidence that the candidate adds value over simple baselines.
proposed_updates: Replace the protocol novelty paragraph's categorical ‘no existing review’ statement with a qualified table comparing Teodoro 2025, Kotewitsch 2024, Bedrač 2024, Minuzzi 2026, and the narrower marker/infection reviews.

Revise the 30-minute post-exercise exclusion. Include immediate samples when they characterize kinetics, but label phase bins and distinguish immediate concentration changes from later functional or clinical vulnerability.

Separate acute exercise challenges, repeated training/adaptation studies, competition/event cohorts, and resting cross-sectional comparisons. Do not treat them as one exposure or infer acute kinetics from chronic studies.

Keep healthy human participants as the core. Chart older adults as a prespecified subgroup; chart disease populations, animal/in-vitro evidence and non-human contexts separately or exclude them explicitly.

Add a two-level endpoint map: biological measures (counts, concentrations, transcript levels) versus demonstrated function (cytotoxicity, proliferation, mucosal function, pathogen response), then separately clinical infection associations and prediction/validation.

Operationalize ‘precision’: baseline-adjusted within-person variation, repeated-measure reliability, population subgroup/moderator analysis, predictive performance and external validation. Label candidates as mechanistic, responsive, function-linked, infection-associated or prediction-validated; do not treat them as equivalent.

Use a broad but explicit omics taxonomy: transcriptomics (including ncRNA), proteomics/extracellular vesicles, metabolomics/lipidomics/immunometabolomics and epigenomics; report when a study is multi-omics versus a single platform.

Before formal registration/search, verify review registrations including CRD42023408388, CRD42021245527, CRD42021244426, CRD42022380991, CRD42024535364, CRD420251042422 and CRD420251236842; identify any newly registered protocol through documented PROSPERO/database searches.
search_limitations: This was a targeted public-web evidence check using search-engine results and opened PubMed/PMC, publisher and journal pages. It was not a full live search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science or SPORTDiscus and did not generate reproducible database exports or PRISMA counts.
PROSPERO was checked through publicly indexed records and identifiers stated by papers, not through a complete saved registry export; lack of a surfaced matching protocol is not evidence none exists.

Some publisher pages were abstract-only or partially accessible; full-text claims were used only where a publisher/PMC full text was available. Sample sizes are null where the source did not state a total participant count.
A targeted correction/retraction search found no obvious notice for the reviewed records, but a comprehensive Crossmark, publisher and retraction-database audit was not performed.
